text: As the manufacture of integrated circuits advances toward smaller sizes and higher integration densities, the requirements for interconnect materials are becoming more stringent, while the limitations of traditional copper interconnection have become increasingly apparent. 1−6 The resistivity of copper interconnects increases exponentially when the width falls below the copper mean free path, primarily due to frequent electron scattering at interfaces and grain boundaries, which becomes the main factor determining the resistivity. 7,8 In contrast, cobalt interconnects possess better properties, such as very short electronic mean free path, relatively low price, and good compatibility in silicon-based electronic chips. 9−11 Besides, cobalt has a higher melting point, which is more beneficial to reduce the electromigration caused by atomic difusion. 12 These properties are particularly beneficial for applications in advanced integrated circuit assemblies in the post-Moore’s law era. Therefore, cobalt is expected to be a new generation of interconnection material instead of traditional copper. 13−15

text: The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing electrodeposition processes for copper damascene interconnects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt filling at present. 16−18 In recent years, the process of copper electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect structures. 19,20

text: The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the additive concentration gradient. 21,22 When the deposition rate at the bottom of the hole is higher than that at the upper part of the hole, it can obtain the void-free superfilling deposition of cobalt in the microvias, holes, or trenches from bottom to to p. 23−25 These additives have efects on controlling the deposition process and have influence on the surface morphology, crystal structure, and electrical properties of the cobalt films. 26−29 The research on cobalt electroplating additives has focused on finding compounds that can achieve superfilling while improving plating properties. However, there are few reports and research studies in this field, particularly for the superfilling processes at present.

text: In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chronopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure. In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

text: 2.4. Electrodeposition. A cobalt plate of 99.99% purity served as the anode. Silicon wafers, measuring 1.5 cm by 1.5 cm, were prepared as cathodes, which were cleaved from a 12 in. diameter silicon wafer with a copper seed layer of 500 nm thickness deposited onto the adhesion layer. Unless otherwise noted, the cobalt films were electrodeposited at a current density of 0.4 ASD with a rotation speed of 500 rpm for a duration of 10 min. Electrodeposition experiments were performed at a constant environmental temperature of 25 ^ ° C. The morphology of cobalt films was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN MIRA3). The surface roughness of the cobalt films was examined by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Oxford Instruments MFP-3D). The crystal structure of the cobalt film was obtained by an X-ray difractometer (XRD, Rigaku Mini Flex 600), operated at 40 kV and 15 mA, in the range from 3 0 ^ ° to 8 0 ^ ° with a step of 0.0 2 ^ °. The depth profiles of various elements in the electrodeposited cobalt films were obtained using time-of flight secondary ion mass spectroscopy (TOF-SIMS, TESCAN GAIA3). The cobalt film sheet resistance was measured via a four-point probe setup. The silicon wafers with copper seed layer used for superfilling were nanometer-scale structures, with a diameter of approximately 100 nm and a high aspect ratio (AR) around 5.

text: 3.4. Cobalt Superfilling. In the electrodeposition process, the constraints of the hole geometry lead to higher electric field and mass-transport conditions at the top of the hole. 36,37 The current and ion concentration at the top of the hole is often higher than at the bottom; as a result, cobalt tends to deposit more rapidly at the top than at the bottom, resulting in the formation of structures containing voids. Besides, as the current density increases, the possibility of void formation also rises, which is attributed to a more pronounced concentration of current at the top of the hole and an increased restriction on mass-transport at the bottom. Therefore, in terms of current parameter settings, the electrodeposition was carried out using segmental currents and starting from a small current (Table 2) in order to optimize the filling process, improve the filling eficiency, and reduce the defects (such as pores and voids) in the process.

text: Based on the above study, cobalt superfilling electrodeposition was performed with AP4A. The cross-sectional view (Figure 5) confirms AP4A’s capability as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling. In this work, the concentration of AP4A is 5 ppm, which achieved bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition. The bottom-up filling mechanism is depicted in Figure 6. During the process of cobalt electrodeposition, AP4A molecules are adsorbed on the surface of the electrode, modulating the partial electric field strength and current density distribution. In addition, under the influence of mass transport, the molecules have a higher concentration at the top of the hole, leading to a more significant inhibitory efect and slowing down the rate of reduction of the cobalt ions. As a result, the electric field and concentration gradient developed in the presence of the AP4A molecules lead to a higher rate of deposition of cobalt ions at the bottom of the hole than at the top, resulting in the expected bottom-up superfilling.
